Should Governments Control Obesity?

The prevalence of obesity in the world has more than doubled in the past 34 years. Over 43 million of the world’s children are obese and many will continue to be obese throughout their lives. The governments of countries such as Canada, the United States, and England have tried to stop the rise in obesity by setting up websites, school programs, and posing restrictions on what can be sold at school. Mexico has passed a sugar tax and a special tax on junk food to try and restrict the consumption of high-calorie, fat, and salt foods. This is all to try and reduce the amount of obesity in these countries and slow the number of obesity cases from rising. Advocates for government action believe that the government should do more to stop the obesity trend; these ideas include bringing more access to healthier food in under-served areas and requiring all institutions to list the nutrition information versus the nutrition requirements. Yet, people are still saying “we want our junk food,” and believe that government does not have a place in controlling what they eat. Therefore, the question is not what government should do to control obesity, but should government do anything at all?

Those who believe that governments should not try to control obesity argue that the bans implemented simply do not work. In 2007, Quebec’s government decided to step in and ban advertising to children; the obesity levels did not change (Points Against.) The argument is made that since Canada did not succeed, then neither would countries with similar climate, region, and population. Sweden also implemented a harsh ban on advertising to children but a direct correlation to obesity rates has not been made. In addition, banning advertisements to children means that millions in revenue are lost every year (Food Advertising.) According to Ben Wolford, countries ban television ads for unhealthy foods aimed at children, but the shows themselves are just as bad. Children’s shows falsely depict that unhealthy foods could be eaten without showing the consequences to their health.

This argument makes an unwarranted assumption in that simply because Canada’s ban did not succeed, neither will other countries. All of the arguments made for this point included Western countries, giving no evidence for other parts of the world. A counterargument could be made that because children now have technology such as smartphones and computers- therefore giving access to content from other countries that do not have a ban on advertising to children- it is not effective to ban advertisements.

Another assertion against governments controlling obesity is that funding attempts at controlling obesity is too much of an issue. Countries like the United States are trillions of dollars in debt and have too many other issues to invest money into to spend money on things such as government campaigns. Around the world, countries have spent billions of dollars trying to stop crime, poverty, teenage pregnancy or drug use, and none of these things have been resolved. If government’s campaigns worked, there would not be anyone using drugs or smoking (Points Against.) It is also claimed that because many governments cannot fund campaigns or more access to healthy food, the money would have to come from the people. The example of Britain, where the PR firm for the government’s food campaign was employed by fast-food giants, is used as another example for why it is a waste of the government’s funds to spend money against obesity (PR Firm).

This source is biased in that it dismisses any examples of government initiatives having an effect on an issue. For example, California funded easier access to contraceptives and sex education campaigns in order to reduce teen pregnancy and it worked, cutting teen pregnancy levels by almost half. There are no statistics provided on how ineffective or effective any government campaigns—against obesity or otherwise—have proven. It is, however, true that many countries lack the funding and initiative to fight obesity levels.

Those who claim that governments do have a place in fighting obesity argue that governments can actually reduce the amount of obesity in their countries. A study based on the United Kingdom (UK) showed that a 20% tax increase on sugary drinks would result in a 1.3% decrease in obesity rates in the UK. It was estimated that the United States could experience as much as a 3% decrease if taxes on sugary drinks were implemented (Overall and Income). It is also argued that hundreds of calories less would be consumed from sugary drinks if a tax were placed. Denmark is often used as an example of a country taking the steps to implement taxes on junk food and foods with high sugar and fat levels in an attempt to lower the amount of obesity prevalent in the country.

Many sources did not consider that Denmark revoked the taxes after it was discovered that many citizens would cross borders in order to get the untaxed products. Denmark also announced that it would no longer be going forward with a tax on sugar. The studies done on the UK are very hypothetical and based on surveys and lack a large amount of hard evidence. It is correct however, that a tax on unhealthy foods could at least reduce the amount of sugar and chemicals people are putting in their bodies. Taxes alone have not been proven to decrease obesity but if governments were to implement other strategies, a change could be made.

It is also asserted by those who want government action that a lot of money could be made and saved by the government if success was reached in the fight against obesity. Countries such as India, France, and Germany could benefit from a decrease in obesity since they offer free health care (Here’s a Map). Expenses for the medical issues that usually come with obesity such as: diabetes, high blood pressure, etc. could be used for other things. The United States would also benefit from less expenses on Medicaid and Medicare for obese people. The effects of a one cent per ounce tax on sugary beverages would raise approximately $15 billion to $20 billion per year (5 Reasons). Those in support of this argument also say that governments would pay a lot less in public health care costs, productivity would increase, and individuals would also see a reduction in health costs (Financial Impacts).

The sources in this argument clearly believe that less obesity would result more money for the government but do not question what that would mean for the population. It is also not questioned what the government would do with this extra money, it is assumed that it would benefit the countries. There is also the use of a slippery slope fallacy in that a lot of sources assume that individuals would be more productive without being obese.

After considering both sides and the reliability of the sources, I believe it is apparent that the government should step into the obesity epidemic. So many children and adults around the world are obese, a problem something that directly impacts their health. As mentioned before, simple taxes on unhealthy food will not solve the problem. People feel it is unconstitutional or a violation of rights if the government intervenes but the health of minors is impacted and billions of dollars are being spent in health care because of obesity. Given that without government intervention, the obesity epidemic will not solve itself, things need to be done and changes need to be made. While I have come to the conclusion that yes, governments should make changes in order to reduce obesity, the continuation of this paper would be to see what the government should do in order to fight obesity. It has become apparent to me during the research of this paper that this health crisis cannot be ignored by governments and people suffering from obesity.

Windows Time Service

Some people have been seeing issues with Windows Time failing to sync properly. This version of Ancile may fix this. To make sure that Windows Time is running correctly, After you have run this version of Ancile run the following command from an administrative prompt:

C:\>w32tm /resync
Sending resync command to local computer
The command completed successfully.

If you get the output above, everything is fine. If you get an error, you will need to fix the Windows Time Service by following the instructions below.

From an administrative prompt run the following commands

C:\>net stop w32time
C:\>w32tm /unregister <-- If this command fails try running it again
C:\>w32tm /register
C:\>net start w32time
C:\>w32tm /resync

If the resync is successful this time then everything has been fixed.
